subtitle: The control unit turns an opcode into the exact sequence of signals that move data through the machine.

micro.body:
When you say “add these two numbers”, the processor does not do it in one gulp. It breaks the instruction into tiny steps, each small enough to fit in one clock tick. These steps are micro-operations, each a register-transfer. Fetch, for example, is four of them: MAR ← PC; MDR ← Memory[MAR]; IR ← MDR; PC ← PC + 1.

What makes each step happen? A control word, the set of signals (which register loads, which bus is driven, what the ALU does) asserted in one step. Think of it as a row of light switches, set one way for each clock tick. The figure shows four micro-operations making up the instruction fetch.
keynotes: An instruction is carried out as a sequence of micro-operations, each a register-transfer that fits in one clock.
Fetch is MAR ← PC; MDR ← Memory[MAR]; IR ← MDR; PC ← PC + 1.
A control word is the set of signals (which register loads, which bus is driven, what the ALU does) asserted in one step.

hard.body:
How do you build the part that sets the switches? One way is with plain logic gates, like wiring a pinball machine: a fixed set of connections that cannot be changed. A hardwired control unit generates signals with combinational logic: a step counter decoded to timing signals T1, T2…, an opcode decoder, and gates that AND them together (e.g. “load IR = T3”).

The main advantage is speed. The price is rigidity: changing the instruction set means redesigning the logic, which is why it is the usual choice for RISC.
keynotes: A hardwired control unit generates signals with combinational logic: a step counter decoded to timing signals, an opcode decoder and gates that AND them together.
It is very fast, but changing the instruction set means redesigning the logic.
It is the usual choice for RISC.

mp.body:
Now imagine, as you design it, building the control unit as a tiny computer of its own, running a program stored in memory. That is the genius of microprogramming. In a microprogrammed unit the control words are stored in a fast control memory. Each instruction’s opcode selects the start of a microroutine; a micro-program counter steps through it, reading one microinstruction per clock and sending its bits to the data path. A microinstruction also says what comes next: fall through, jump, or branch on a condition flag.

Changing or extending the instruction set is just rewriting the microcode (Wilkes’ original idea), which is why CISC designers like it. Size one up: a machine has 64 micro-routines of at most 16 microinstructions each and 40 control signals. The control memory holds 64 × 16 = 1024 words, and each word carries the 40 signals plus a next-address field of ⌈log₂1024⌉ = 10 bits, so 1024 × 50 = 51200 bits.
keynotes: In a microprogrammed unit the control words are stored in a fast control memory; the opcode selects a microroutine and a micro-program counter steps through it, one microinstruction per clock.
Changing or extending the instruction set is just rewriting the microcode (Wilkes’ idea), which is why CISC machines use it.
64 micro-routines of up to 16 microinstructions with 40 signals and a 10-bit next-address field need 51200 bits of control memory.

horiz.body: How wide should a microinstruction be? There is a choice, and it is the old trade of speed against size. Horizontal microinstructions give every control signal its own bit: wide, fast, and highly parallel. Vertical ones encode the signals in fields (like opcodes) and need decoders: narrow but slower. Real designs mix them. A horizontal microinstruction is therefore a wide word with one bit per control signal.
keynotes: Horizontal microinstructions give every control signal its own bit: wide, fast, highly parallel.
Vertical ones encode the signals in fields and need decoders: narrow but slower.

seq.body:
After each microinstruction, how does the control unit know (and how would you decide) what to run next? It has its own little program counter logic, and the next address comes from one of several sources: the incremented µPC (most steps), a jump field, a conditional branch on a flag, a mapping from the opcode (at the start), or a stack for microsubroutines.

The figure shows a conditional microbranch. Which source normally supplies the next microaddress? The incremented µPC, just as an ordinary program normally runs the next line.
keynotes: The next microaddress comes from the incremented µPC (most steps), a jump field, a conditional branch on a flag, a mapping from the opcode, or a stack for microsubroutines.
Address generation is the control unit’s own program counter logic.
Normally the incremented µPC supplies the next microaddress.

summary.body:
Three ideas to carry away, and you will find them again in the memory chapter.

  • Instructions = sequences of micro-operations; a control word drives one step.
  • Hardwired: fast, rigid. Microprogrammed: flexible, a bit slower.
  • Horizontal = wide and parallel; vertical = narrow and encoded.
keynotes: Instructions are sequences of micro-operations and a control word drives one step.
Hardwired control is fast and rigid; microprogrammed control is flexible and a bit slower.
Horizontal microcode is wide and parallel; vertical is narrow and encoded.
